newsitem.title: USA: Big crop, mild weather hits orange juice prices.
newsitem.headline: Big crop, mild weather hits orange juice prices.

text.p: Frozen concentrated orange juice prices fell sharply Friday on forecasts of spring-like weather in Florida, bolstering prospects for a bumper orange crop.

Crude oil futures rose in New York after two reports showed greater-than-expected decreases in stocks of U.S. crude, heating oil and diesel fuel last week. Heating oil prices also rose on the data despite forecasts for warmer weather that could lower consumption.
Orange juice prices slid nearly the 5 cent daily limit in several contracts at the New York Cotton Exchange and set contract lows in all contract months.
A record Florida orange crop is projected next year, and warm weather forecast throughout the citrus belt weighed heavily on Friday's market.
Buzz Lopez, an assistant meteorologist with Smith Barney, said Florida temperatures will remain in the 50s and 60s for the next six to 10 days.
"There is no indication of any cool air going into Florida," Lopez said. "There may be a cooldown next week, but temperatures will remain in the upper 40s."
The Agriculture Department estimates the next Florida crop at 220 million 90-pound boxes vs. 203.2 million this past year.

The actively traded March frozen concentrated orange juice contract was down 4 cents at a contract low of 81.85 cents per pound. The January contract was off 4.30 cents at 78.10 after sliding to a contract low of 78.00.
Crude oil prices rose at the New York Mercantile Exchange after weekly oil inventory data showed unexpected drawdowns in crude, heating oil and diesel stocks.
"We had some high draws in crude and distillate stocks which really caught people off guard," said Jeff Foose, a dealer with KCS Energy in New Jersey.
Late Thursday, the American Petroleum Institute reported distillate stocks declined 1.89 million barrels during the week ended Dec. 20. Distillates include heating oil and diesel.
Crude stocks fell 5.16 million barrels while gasoline stocks grew by 504,000 barrels.
The Energy Information Administration reported a reduction of 300,000 barrels in gasoline stocks in its own weekly inventory data Thursday, as well as reductions in distillates and crude.
Heating oil prices were seen as being on shaky ground due to forecasts for unseasonably warm weather, which is expected to ease demand in the key Northeast heating oil market.

Weather Services Corp. forecast above-average temperatures through the weekend in the Northeast, and the National Weather Service's six- to 10-day forecast called for normal temperatures in the region. Dealers had expected colder weather.

On the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for February delivery settled 30 cents higher at $25.22 a barrel. January heating oil ended 0.49 cent a gallon higher at 70.55 cents, while January gasoline finished 0.23 cent higher at 69.74 cents a gallon.
Coffee futures rose to a four-month high at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange on aggressive buying by speculative funds.
"There was very good fund buying," said one trader, noting that traders connected with world producers were absent. "Colombia and Brazil weren't there. Everyone is on vacation."

Underpinning Friday's gains were expectations of a smaller Brazil coffee crop next year. On Thursday, officials from Minais Gerais state in Brazil estimated the 1997-98 crop at 8.3 million bags, down from a revised 13.8 million in 1996-97.
CSCE March coffee rose 1.45 cents to 116.20 cents per pound.
